summary: The Roof shingle calculator turns the roof length, the roof width and more into roof area in squares. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Roof shingle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Roof shingle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports roof area in squares in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the roof length, the roof width, the roof pitch (%) and the one bundle roof coverage.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Roof shingle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Roof area in squares=(1 ÷ 100) × roof area
Shingle bundles=rounded up, (roof area ÷ one bundle roof coverage)
Footprint area=roof length × roof width
Footprint area=roof area ÷ (((1 ÷ 12) × the square root of ((roof pitch (x:12) ^ 2) + 144)))
Bundle size=shingles ÷ rounded up, (roof area ÷ one bundle roof coverage)
Multiplier=((1 ÷ 12) × the square root of ((roof pitch (x:12) ^ 2) + 144))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Roof pitch (x:12) = 2, One bundle roof coverage = 0.0002 m² and Bundle size = 29 — it reports Roof pitch (%) = 16.6667 %, Roof pitch (angle) = 9.4623 deg and Multiplier = 1.0138.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Roof pitch (%) = 16.6667 %, Roof pitch (angle) = 9.4623 deg and Multiplier = 1.0138 should be roughly the size you expected from Roof pitch (x:12) = 2 and One bundle roof coverage = 0.0002 m².

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • %, opening in percent
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Area, opening in square meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Roof shingle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the roof length, the roof width and the roof pitch — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Roof shingle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns roof area in squares, derived from the roof length, the roof width and the roof pitch. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Roof shingle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the roof length, the roof width, the roof pitch and the one bundle roof coverage, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter roof length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Roof length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Roof pitch (%) = 16.6667 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Roof shingle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
